trap.wrong: "A fixed limit of N requests per minute per IP."
trap.why: Fixed windows punish bursty but well-behaved clients and allow double the limit around window boundaries; IPs don't map to tenants.
trap.probe: Token bucket with burst, per-tenant keys, local approximation, clear 429s, a global safety layer.
trap.say: "A token bucket per tenant (sustained rate plus burst) backed by a shared store with local approximation, 429 with Retry-After, and global load shedding underneath."

thesis: Use token buckets per tenant: a sustained rate plus a burst allowance, so short spikes from good clients pass while sustained abuse is limited. Keep counters in a fast shared store with local approximation to avoid a round trip per request, return clear 429s with Retry-After, and tier quotas by plan.
pitch: Fixed-window limits punish bursty clients: a client that sends 100 requests in one second and nothing for the rest of the minute looks abusive. A token bucket fits better: tokens refill at the sustained rate, the bucket holds a burst capacity, and each request takes a token. Good clients with occasional bursts never notice; a client sending at a sustained high rate drains the bucket and gets limited. I'd key buckets by tenant and optionally by endpoint class, since writes or expensive endpoints get tighter limits. For a distributed fleet, the state lives in Redis or similar, updated atomically with a script, but calling Redis on every request adds latency, so I'd have each instance hold a local share of the tenant's budget and sync periodically, accepting small overshoot. Responses include 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers showing remaining quota. Limits come from the tenant's plan, and I'd add a global concurrency or load-shedding layer above it, because per-tenant limits don't protect you if every tenant bursts at once.

points.d: Refill rate = sustained limit; bucket size = burst allowance. A request consumes tokens; an empty bucket means 429.

points.h: Key by tenant and cost class
points.d: Separate buckets for cheap reads and expensive writes or reports, or weight requests by cost.
Atomic token updates in Redis (Lua scripts) give a fleet-wide view. Plan for Redis being unavailable: fail open with local limits, usually.
Each instance gets a slice of the tenant's budget or syncs counts every few hundred milliseconds. Cuts latency and load on the store, at the cost of slight overshoot.
429 with Retry-After, plus headers for limit, remaining and reset. Document the limits so clients can design for them.
Limits by plan, with overrides for specific tenants and a process for temporary increases.
Per-tenant limits don't cap total load. Keep service-wide admission control and load shedding too.

decision: Token bucket per tenant with burst headroom for API rate limits; concurrency limits for long-running or expensive operations; global load shedding underneath. Fail open on limiter outages for most APIs, closed for abuse-prone endpoints such as login.
numbers: Example plan: 100 requests/s sustained with a burst of 500. A client sending 400 requests in one second after being idle passes; sustained 200 requests/s drains the bucket within a few seconds and is limited to 100/s.
Local approximation: with 20 instances syncing every 250 ms, worst-case overshoot is roughly the tokens consumed in one sync interval across instances.
pitfalls: Fixed one-minute windows allowing double the limit around window boundaries and punishing bursts.
Per-IP limits for B2B APIs where many tenants share NAT gateways, or one tenant uses many IPs.
A Redis round trip on every request in the hot path.
429s without Retry-After, causing clients to retry immediately.

followups.a: Sliding window counters are good for 'N per period' quotas (daily limits); token bucket is better for rate plus burst behaviour. Many systems use both: a token bucket for rate, a daily quota for volume.

followups.q: What happens when Redis is down?
followups.a: Fall back to per-instance local limits (limit divided by instance count) so you neither block everyone nor remove protection entirely.

followups.q: How do you rate-limit fairly when overloaded?
followups.a: Combine per-tenant limits with weighted fair queueing or shedding by tenant share, so a big tenant can't take all remaining capacity.

example: A B2B API moved from 6,000 requests per minute fixed windows to a token bucket of 100/s with a 1,000-token burst. Batch jobs that sent spikes at the top of each hour stopped getting 429s, while a misbehaving client looping at 400/s was held to 100/s.
